title: 1 Samuel 16:1–13
context: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse’s sons, telling him to bring a heifer for a sacrifice so as not to alarm Saul. When Samuel sees the tall eldest son, Eliab, he assumes he is the one, but the LORD tells him that he looks at the heart, not the outward appearance. Seven sons pass by without being chosen. The youngest, David, is called in from the sheep, and the LORD tells Samuel to anoint him. From that day the Spirit of the LORD comes mightily on David.

verses.text: The LORD said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks how long Samuel will mourn for Saul and sends him to Jesse in Bethlehem. Arminian readers see God moving Samuel from grief to action, with the future of the kingdom still in God’s care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase “I have provided a king for myself,” a contrast with the people’s demand for a king in chapter 8. Both traditions read the verse as God taking the initiative to choose the next king himself.

verses.text: Samuel said, “How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me.” The LORD said, “Take a heifer with you, and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.’
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel fears Saul will kill him, and the LORD tells him to bring a heifer and say he has come to sacrifice. Arminian readers note that the stated purpose is true, though not the whole purpose, and they discuss this carefully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note that the sacrifice is real and that God directs what is disclosed. Shared ground: both traditions see the instruction as protecting Samuel without requiring a false statement, though readers discuss the ethics of concealment.

verses.text: Call Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. You shall anoint to me him whom I name to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Samuel to invite Jesse to the sacrifice and promises to show him whom to anoint. Arminian readers note that Samuel must wait for God’s guidance step by step, rather than relying on his own judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the choice of the king resting entirely in God’s naming. Both traditions read the verse as preparing for the lesson of 16:7, where Samuel’s own assumptions will be corrected by the LORD.

verses.text: Samuel did that which the LORD spoke, and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling, and said, “Do you come peaceably?”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel comes to Bethlehem, and the elders meet him trembling, asking if he comes in peace. Arminian readers note that the prophet’s arrival causes fear, perhaps because of his role in judgment or his recent break with Saul.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the elders’ trembling as reflecting respect for the prophet’s authority. Shared ground: the text does not say why they fear, and both traditions avoid speculating beyond what the verse reports.

verses.text: He said, “Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Sanctify yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice.” He sanctified Jesse and his sons, and called them to the sacrifice.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says he comes peaceably and invites them to consecrate themselves for the sacrifice, and he consecrates Jesse and his sons. Arminian readers note the care taken to prepare the family for worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Samuel’s personal role in consecrating Jesse’s sons as setting the stage for God’s choice. Both traditions read the verse as placing the anointing within an act of worship, not as a political maneuver.

verses.text: When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, “Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel sees Eliab and thinks he must be the LORD’s anointed. Arminian readers note that even a faithful prophet can misjudge when he relies on appearances, as Israel did with Saul’s height (9:2; 10:23).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as preparing to show that God’s choice does not follow human expectations. Shared ground: Samuel’s assumption is natural, and the verse sets up the correction that follows immediately in 16:7.

verses.text: But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he does not see as man sees; man looks at outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart. Arminian readers see God valuing the inner disposition and responsiveness of the person he chooses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s choice as sovereign and not based on human measures of worth. Shared ground: both traditions treat this verse as a central and agreed truth, that God judges by the heart rather than by outward appearance.

verses.text: Then Jesse called Abinadab, and made him pass before Samuel. He said, “The LORD has not chosen this one, either.”
verses.arminianNotes: Abinadab passes before Samuel, but the LORD has not chosen him. Arminian readers note the patient process, as each son is presented and Samuel waits on God’s word for each one in turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated refusals as underlining that the choice belongs to God alone. Both traditions read the sequence as a lesson that human order, such as birth order, does not determine whom God calls.

verses.text: Then Jesse made Shammah to pass by. He said, “The LORD has not chosen this one, either.”
verses.arminianNotes: Shammah passes by, and he too is not chosen. Arminian readers note that Samuel’s earlier mistake has made him attentive, so he now waits for God’s direction instead of judging by appearances.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition building suspense toward the unexpected choice. Shared ground: the brief verse continues the pattern of refusal, emphasizing that none of the expected candidates is the one God has chosen.

verses.text: Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. Samuel said to Jesse, “The LORD has not chosen these.”
verses.arminianNotes: Seven of Jesse’s sons pass before Samuel, and none is chosen. Arminian readers note that Samuel is left puzzled, since God’s promise in 16:1 seems unfulfilled until he asks about the absent son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the number seven as completing the expected candidates, so that the choice falls outside them. Both traditions read the verse as setting up the surprise that the chosen king is the one not even invited.

verses.text: Samuel said to Jesse, “Are all your children here?” He said, “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and get him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel asks if all the sons are present, and Jesse mentions the youngest, keeping the sheep. Arminian readers note that David was overlooked even by his own father, who did not think to include him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God choosing the least likely, a pattern seen elsewhere in Scripture. Shared ground: the shepherd image anticipates David’s role as shepherd of Israel (2 Samuel 5:2), and both traditions read the detail with that in view.

verses.text: He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. The LORD said, “Arise! Anoint him, for this is he.”
verses.arminianNotes: David is brought in, ruddy and handsome, and the LORD says to anoint him. Arminian readers note that David is described as good-looking, so the point of 16:7 is not that appearance is bad, but that it is not decisive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word, “this is he,” as the decisive factor in the choice. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the LORD, not Samuel or Jesse, identifies the king, while the description of David remains positive.

verses.text: Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the middle of his brothers. Then the LORD’s Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel anoints David, and the LORD’s Spirit comes mightily on him from that day. Arminian readers note that the same language was used of Saul (10:10; 11:6), and see the Spirit equipping David for his calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Spirit’s coming as God’s empowering of his chosen king for the task ahead. Shared ground: both traditions read the anointing and the Spirit together as marking David as the LORD’s choice, though his reign lies years ahead.
